rounds.root_cause: The label in this data is driven largely by topic, not by sentiment wording: sports/athletics texts are labeled positive even when heavily hedged ('fairly decent, but uncertain', 'marginally better, however concerns remain'), while business/workplace/technical texts are labeled negative even when they contain positive elements ('foundation appears solid', 'reasonable progress overall'), and purely factual neutral statements ('The meeting was scheduled...', 'facility operates during current hours') are also labeled negative. The single holistic element reads surface sentiment, so it is fooled by hedged sports texts (calls them negative) and by neutral or mixed business texts (calls them positive), which is exactly the error split seen in all 25 disagreements. A topic feature plus an explicit-evaluation feature give the decision model the axes the label actually uses.

proposed.instructions: Is this text about sports, athletics, a sports team, or athletic training or competition?
Does this text express any evaluative judgment (positive or negative) about its subject, rather than only stating neutral facts, schedules, or procedures?

rounds.root_cause: The label is not pure sentiment: in the labeled sample every sports/recreational text is positive while dry business/technical procedural texts are negative, and in mixed texts the label follows the main clause while the concession after 'however/but/still/though' is a distractor. The single holistic question cannot see topic at all, and it latches onto the concessive clause, so it calls neutral business statements and 'not quite... but solid' statements positive (21 of 25 errors) and misses hedged sports positives. Adding a topic element and a main-clause-sentiment element attacks both failure modes.

proposed.instructions: Is this text about sports, athletics, exercise, or recreational physical activities (for example a team, training, match, venue, or equipment used for sport)?

Ignoring any concession introduced by words like 'however', 'but', 'still', 'though', 'although' or 'nonetheless', what is the sentiment of the text's main point? Answer 'no_clear_sentiment' if the text is purely factual or procedural with no evaluation.

rounds.root_cause: The human labels track topic far more than sentiment: in both the labeled sample and the disagreements, sports texts are labeled positive and workplace/procedural texts are labeled negative, even when their wording points the other way. The scorecard has a sports-topic detector but nothing that recognizes the business/procedural texts that make up the negative class, so those texts fall through to the positive-leaning prior, especially when main_clause_sentiment reads them as 'positive' or 'no_clear_sentiment' or element answers are missing. The bulk of the disagreements are exactly this: non-sports procedural texts predicted positive, plus a few sports texts where negative wording overrode the topic signal.

proposed.instructions: Is this text about workplace, business, technical, or administrative matters (for example reports, protocols, compliance, maintenance, scheduling, procedures, deliverables, or resource management)?

rounds.root_cause: Two error clusters dominate. First, in contrastive two-clause texts the label follows the first evaluative clause (the part before 'however/but/while/still'), but main_clause_sentiment keeps judging the post-contrast clause or gives up with 'no_clear_sentiment' -- the question never says which clause is the concession. Second, a large set of purely procedural statements ('X was coordinated according to guidelines', 'reports were assigned by administration') are labeled negative in this data, yet the element layer has no explicit 'this is neutral/procedural' signal: main_clause_sentiment often calls them 'positive' (misreading 'conforms'/'coordinated' as evaluation) and the topic features misfire, so the fit has nothing reliable to attach the neutral->negative convention to.

proposed.instructions: Is this text a purely factual, procedural, or administrative statement that reports an action, arrangement, or status without evaluating anything as good or bad (for example that something was scheduled, assigned, distributed, coordinated, reviewed, or maintained according to some procedure)?

rounds.root_cause: No scorecard, disagreement comments, or permutation importance data were provided in this round, so there is no evidence from which to identify a pattern of errors. Per the operating rules, when the evidence does not support any change, the correct action is to propose nothing rather than invent edits.

The scorecard relies on a single holistic sentiment answer, and that answer is systematically fooled by concession-structured texts: it latches onto the softening clause ('it did manage to cover most essential components', 'the foundation appears solid', 'sustainability is questionable') instead of the main evaluation. In the labeled sample the label consistently follows the primary evaluative clause, not the 'but/even so/nonetheless' tail -- business texts whose main clause states a shortcoming are negative despite positive concessions (8 of the 25 errors), and sports texts whose main clause is mildly positive are positive despite negative caveats (the gymnastics error). A question that isolates the main point from the concession should correct this whole cluster; the remaining template-sentence errors show no consistent textual rule and look like label noise.

proposed.instructions: Setting aside any softening concession or caveat introduced by words like 'but', 'yet', 'even so', 'nonetheless', 'while', or 'though', is the text's main point or primary evaluation fundamentally positive (approving, adequate, improving) or negative (criticizing, falling short, concerning)?

rounds.root_cause: The label in this data is driven by conventions the single holistic question cannot see: contrastive texts are labeled by the critical first clause (the model instead follows the upbeat 'however...' tail and says positive), and entire topic groups carry fixed labels (sports/athletics texts are positive even when hedged; routine office/administrative procedure texts are negative even when neutral). With only one feature, the model averages these cues and lands on the wrong side for both groups. Adding explicit elements for the concession structure and for these topic classes gives the fit the signals it currently lacks.

proposed.instructions: If this text contains a contrast or concession (using words like however, although, while, on the other hand, nevertheless, despite), which side carries the overall evaluative stance: the critical or qualified side, or the reassuring or positive side? If there is no contrast, answer none.
Is this text about sports, athletics, exercise, or a team or individual physical activity (such as swimming, soccer, cricket, wrestling, baseball, dance fitness, or track)?

Is this text a routine administrative, facilities, or office-operations statement (for example about onboarding, orientation, conferences, planning sessions, office supplies, break rooms, procurement, or finance protocols) with no strong praise or criticism?

Does the text open with or lean on an uncertainty hedge such as possibly, arguably, potentially, presumably, ostensibly, somewhat, or not entirely sure, so that its overall stance is doubtful or reserved rather than committal?

rounds.root_cause: Two systematic patterns drive the errors. First, a large cluster of bland administrative/facilities/procedural statements (conferences, onboarding, planning sessions, break rooms, parking layouts, documentation, protocols) is labeled negative by humans, but the holistic read scores them positive and the admin_procedure_topic element barely fires (7-17% yes on clear cases) because its question is compound - it asks the model to judge topic AND the absence of praise/criticism at once - so it sits unused with near-zero importance. Second, in contrast/concession sentences the label consistently follows the evaluative polarity of the FIRST clause (e.g. 'While the feedback not quite, there were some encouraging signs' is negative; 'slightly improved, yet several concerns remain' is positive), but concession_lean asks which side carries the 'overall' stance, which the model reasonably answers as the reassuring side, pushing these to positive.

The scorecard relies on a single holistic sentiment read, and on mixed or hedged texts it latches onto the wrong clause: it predicts negative for sports texts that lead with an encouraging evaluation ('hockey session was somewhat encouraging, on the other hand...') and positive for business texts that lead with a criticism but end on a conciliatory note ('proposal slightly underwhelming... yet showed reasonable progress'). The human labels consistently follow the FIRST evaluative claim, not the concession after 'yet/nevertheless/even so'; the labeled sample confirms this (e.g., 'wasn't completely overwhelming' -> positive, 'room for improvement, nevertheless... positive elements' -> negative). An explicit element locating the primary evaluative claim gives the model the feature it needs to stop being swayed by the contrasting tail.

proposed.instructions: Ignoring any contrasting concession introduced by words like 'but', 'yet', 'though', 'even so', 'nevertheless' or 'on the other hand', is the first or main evaluative claim of this text favorable, unfavorable, or is there no evaluative claim?

rounds.root_cause: In mixed-sentiment texts the label consistently follows the FIRST evaluative statement, and the later concession or contrast clause is a distractor (e.g. 'While the client call not quite, there were some encouraging signs' is negative; 'traces of improved balance, even if... shaky' is positive). The single holistic element averages both clauses or locks onto the wrong one, so it confidently flips exactly these cases, which make up the majority of the disagreements. A feature capturing the polarity of the opening assessment gives the model the deciding signal directly.

proposed.instructions: Identify the first statement in the text that evaluates something (expresses approval, disapproval, success, failure, or uncertainty about quality). Ignoring any later contrasting or concessive statement, is that first evaluative statement positive or negative? Answer 'neutral' only if the text contains no evaluative statement at all.

rounds.root_cause: The label in this data tracks topic, not evaluative language: every sports/athletics text in the disagreements and the labeled sample is human-labeled positive (even heavily hedged ones like 'wasn't completely disorganized' or 'consistency remains questionable'), while every business/operations/administrative text is human-labeled negative (even ones with 'encouraging signs' or 'addressed most of the key concerns'). The scorecard has no topic element, so opening_assessment_sentiment keys on exactly the surface sentiment these mixed, concessive texts use to mislead, flipping predictions confidently in both directions. Adding a topic question gives the fit the deciding signal it currently lacks.

proposed.instructions: What is the main subject matter of this text? Answer 'sports' if it concerns sports, athletics, exercise, games, or physical training; 'operations' if it concerns workplace, business, technical, or administrative processes and activities; 'other' if neither applies.

rounds.root_cause: The label tracks the first evaluative statement: concessive texts like 'While X fell short, there were encouraging signs' are negative and 'X improved, though issues remain' are positive, which is exactly what opening_assessment_sentiment asks, but it is being answered like an overall summary -- on 'While...' fragments, hedged first judgments ('marginally better', 'slightly underwhelming', 'traces of improvement') and double negatives ('wasn't completely disorganized') it answers positive or neutral by absorbing the later concession. That single misanswer drives nearly all disagreements, since topic_domain and the intercept then go uncorrected. The holistic feature stays in place (the fit can shrink it); the four 'catastrophe/failure' errors had no element answers at all, and the reworded element covers them whenever it is actually answered.
